query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the concentration of chromium in a high-entropy alloy improves its oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a protective chromium oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a nominal composition rich in Ni, Co, and Fe and a baseline level of Cr (around 18 wt.% as in the referenced HEA).
generation.intervention: Increase the Cr content in the alloy composition while keeping other alloying elements constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environment (e.g., air exposure at elevated temperatures, such as around 800 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent chromium oxide (Cr2O3) film that forms on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Chromium oxidizes preferentially at high temperatures to form a stable Cr2O3 layer that acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby slowing down oxidation and corrosion of the underlying metal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with increased Cr content will display slower oxidation kinetics, evidenced by reduced weight gain or thinner oxide scales, as compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Alloy with a lower or baseline Cr content (e.g., ~18 wt.% Cr) that forms a less effective protective oxide scale under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be effective under high-temperature conditions where oxidation is active and provided that other elements do not adversely affect the integrity of the oxide scale; the benefit may be limited if Cr levels lead to unwanted phase formation or if exposed environments promote volatile oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of oxidation resistance improvement and the optimal Cr concentration require further quantification, as interactions with other alloying elements and processing conditions may influence the protective oxide formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the baseline Cr content (~18 wt.%) and another with an increased Cr content. Expose both sample sets to a high-temperature oxidation test in air (e.g., 800 °C for 100 hours).
measurements: Weight gain (thermogravimetric analysis) as a measure of oxidation rate
Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via SEM and EDS)
Phase identification of the oxide layer (using XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased Cr content does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (e.g., lower weight gain, thinner or more continuous oxide scale) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
